## Which Picture for Which Data? {.ojs-slide #chart-choice}

::: {.lede-min}
Tick the display that suits each set of data. The reasoning appears underneath.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Short labels so all five fit on ONE line at 21px. The fuller names
// (stem-and-leaf, pie) live in the reasoning underneath, where there is room.
ccOpts = ["Bar or pie", "Histogram", "Scatter plot", "Time series", "Box plot"]

// Exercise 1 of the beamer Seminar 1, answers and reasoning carried over.
ccQ = [
  {q: "The tax paid by a light engineering company and its annual profit, for 20 consecutive years.",
   a: "Scatter plot",
   hint: "Look again at how many measures there are, and at what pairs them up.",
   why: "Two numerical measures, and the question is whether they move together. The twenty years supply the pairs, they are not the thing being plotted."},
  {q: "The types of premises occupied by all the small businesses in a town: office, factory, warehouse, and so on.",
   a: "Bar or pie",
   hint: "Ask first whether any of this can go on a number line at all.",
   why: "The variable is categorical. There is nothing to put on a number line, only counts in named boxes, so a bar chart or a pie chart."},
  {q: "The salary of a trainee accountant in the first year of training, at 30 major accountancy firms.",
   a: "Histogram",
   hint: "One measure, thirty values of it, and the shape is what you are after.",
   why: "One numerical measure, and what you want to see is the shape of its spread. A stem-and-leaf does the same job by hand and keeps the digits."},
  {q: "The number of trainee accountants enrolling for professional examinations each year since 1960.",
   a: "Time series",
   hint: "There is one measure here, but it is useless without the year beside it.",
   why: "One measure again, but it only means anything read against the year it belongs to."},
  {q: "The years of experience and the current salary of a random sample of economists at a New York bank.",
   a: "Scatter plot",
   hint: "Count the measures recorded for each economist.",
   why: "Two numerical measures per person, so each economist is one point."}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// What each display is FOR. A wrong answer is explained by naming the job the
// chosen chart actually does, which is one line per option rather than one
// per (question, wrong option) pair — twenty of those would say the same five
// things over and over.
ccJob = ({
  "Bar or pie":   "A bar or pie chart compares counts across named categories",
  "Histogram":    "A histogram shows the shape of one numerical measure",
  "Scatter plot": "A scatter plot shows how two numerical measures move together",
  "Time series":  "A time series plot follows one measure against time",
  "Box plot":     "A box plot summarises the spread of one numerical measure"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Every example plot is real worksheet data, so the picture a student sees
// here is one they meet again later in the module:
//   R&D spend            Seminar 1, Exercise 3   (also slides 8 and 9)
//   Executive pay        Seminar 1, Exercise 2
//   Executive salaries   Seminar 1, Exercise 4   (the stem-and-leaf one)
//   Y against X          Seminar 8, Exercise 2
//   Monthly demand       Seminar 9, Exercise 1
ccStyle = ({fontSize: "13px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
            color: "#6E7681", background: "transparent"})

ccRD = [6.0, 10.4, 10.5, 9.0, 7.3, 6.6, 6.9, 8.2, 7.1, 8.1,
        7.9, 6.8, 7.4, 9.5, 8.1, 13.5, 9.9, 6.9, 11.1, 8.2,
        8.0, 7.7, 7.4, 6.5, 9.5, 8.2, 6.9, 7.2, 8.2, 6.7]

ccSalary = [846, 457, 563, 1466, 1200, 2164, 746, 1611, 824, 824, 1310,
            1007, 1367, 575, 1252, 1354, 2479, 1238, 927, 1253, 925,
            1284, 1279, 1660, 860]

// Five of the twenty-six, all with SHORT names. The bar chart is the only
// plot with words on its y axis, so it used to set the shared left margin at
// 88 — which left the other four, and the box plot worst of all, with a band
// of empty space down their left side and the drawing pushed off centre.
// Picking short names lets every plot share a 44px margin instead.
ccPay = [["CBS", 60.25], ["Exxon", 34.90], ["AT&T", 21.00],
         ["Apple", 4.17], ["Tesco", 1.90]].map(([k, v]) => ({k, v}))

ccPairs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].map((x, i) => ({x, y: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128][i]}))

ccMonths = [23, 39, 36, 26, 36, 12, 26, 30, 42, 35, 36, 28]
  .map((x, i) => ({month: i + 1, x}))

// One geometry for all five: identical margins mean the axes are the same
// length and the ticks the same size from plot to plot, so clicking between
// displays changes the picture and nothing else. marginLeft is set by the
// longest company name on the bar chart; the numeric plots spend that space
// on their y-axis label.
ccBase = ({
  width: 400, height: 152,
  marginTop: 10, marginRight: 16, marginBottom: 56, marginLeft: 66,
  style: ccStyle
})

// labelOffset 38 against a 48 bottom margin: Plot's default sets the axis
// label directly under the tick text and the two touched.
// The two labelOffsets are not equal because they are not measured the same
// way: Plot pushes the x label DOWN from the axis and the y label LEFT from
// it, past tick text of different lengths. These two land both labels the
// same distance clear of their tick numbers, which is what reads as even.
ccAxX = (label) => ({label, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 46, tickSize: 5})
ccAxY = (label, ticks, domain) => ({label, labelAnchor: "center",
                                    labelOffset: 55, tickSize: 5,
                                    ticks, domain, grid: true})
// Explicit tick values, not a count. The shared geometry leaves a 94px plot
// area and `ticks: n` is only a HINT — d3 rounds to a nice step, so both 4
// and 5 came back with six labels 15px apart under 13px type, all but
// touching, while leaving it automatic dropped to two. Naming the values is
// the only way to fix the pitch, and these datasets never change.

ccDemo = ({
  "Bar or pie": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("Executive pay ($m)"),
    y: {label: null, tickSize: 5},
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(ccPay, {y: "k", x: "v", fill: "#325D88",
        sort: {y: "x", reverse: true}}),
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#B0B7C0"})
    ]}),
  "Histogram": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("R&D spend (% of revenue)"),
    y: ccAxY("Firms", [0, 4, 8]),
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(ccRD, Plot.binX({y: "count"},
        {x: d => d, thresholds: d3.range(6, 15), fill: "#325D88"})),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#B0B7C0"})
    ]}),
  "Scatter plot": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: ccAxX("X"), y: ccAxY("Y", [0, 40, 80, 120]),
    marks: [Plot.dot(ccPairs, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#325D88", r: 3.4})]}),
  "Time series": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: {...ccAxX("Month"), tickFormat: "d"}, // From zero: a demand axis that starts at 15 exaggerates every dip.
    y: ccAxY("Demand", [0, 25, 50], [0, 50]),
    marks: [Plot.line(ccMonths, {x: "month", y: "x",
      stroke: "#325D88", strokeWidth: 2})]}),
  "Box plot": () => Plot.plot({...ccBase,
    x: {...ccAxX("Executive salary (£000s)"), grid: true},
    y: {label: null, ticks: [], tickSize: 5},
    marks: [Plot.boxX(ccSalary, {x: d => d, fill: "#CBD9E6", stroke: "#325D88"})]})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccIcon = {
  const NAVY = "#325D88";
  const wrap = inner =>
    `<svg width="42" height="26" viewBox="0 0 42 26" aria-hidden="true">${inner}</svg>`;
  // Bars on a 40-wide strip sitting on a baseline at y = 22. A histogram's
  // bars touch and a bar chart's do not, which is the one difference a
  // student is meant to read off these thumbnails.
  const bars = (hs, pitch, w) => hs.map((h, i) =>
    `<rect x="${2 + i * pitch}" y="${22 - h}" width="${w}" height="${h}" fill="${NAVY}"/>`
  ).join("");
  const line = (x1, y1, x2, y2) =>
    `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>`;
  return ({
    "Bar or pie": wrap(bars([16, 9, 13, 6], 10, 7)),
    "Histogram": wrap(bars([5, 12, 18, 11, 5], 8, 8)),
    "Scatter plot": wrap([[5,20],[11,16],[16,18],[21,13],[26,11],[32,8],[38,5]]
      .map(([x, y]) => `<circle cx="${x}" cy="${y}" r="2.1" fill="${NAVY}"/>`).join("")),
    "Time series": wrap(
      `<polyline points="3,20 10,12 17,16 24,7 31,11 39,4" fill="none"
         stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/>`),
    "Box plot": wrap(line(3, 13, 12, 13) + line(28, 13, 39, 13) +
      `<rect x="12" y="7" width="16" height="12" fill="none" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>` +
      line(21, 7, 21, 19))
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ccI = Inputs.radio([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {value: 1, label: "Question"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccPrompt = html`<div class="quiz-q">${ccQ[ccI - 1].q}</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ccPick = {
  ccI;   // naming it here rebuilds the input when the question changes, which
         // is the only way to clear the previous answer's ticks
  // html([...]) rather than html`...`: the sketch is a string of markup and
  // the tagged form would escape it into visible angle brackets.
  // radio, not checkbox: every question has exactly one right display, so
  // letting the room tick three of them only invites a wrong kind of answer.
  return Inputs.radio(ccOpts, {
    label: "Suitable display",
    format: v => html([`<span class="quiz-opt">${ccIcon[v]}<span>${v}</span></span>`])
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ccFeedback = {
  const want = ccQ[ccI - 1].a;
  if (!ccPick) return html`<div class="quiz-fb quiz-idle">Pick a display to see the reasoning.</div>`;
  const ok = ccPick === want;
  // A wrong pick names the job the chosen chart does and points back at the
  // data. It does NOT name the answer: handing it over ends the thinking, and
  // the radio is still there to try again with.
  const text = ok
    ? html`<b>Yes.</b> ${ccQ[ccI - 1].why}`
    : html`<b>Not quite.</b> ${ccJob[ccPick]}. ${ccQ[ccI - 1].hint}`;
  // The plot always shows the display that was PICKED, not the right one —
  // on a wrong answer it is the thing they asked for, which is an argument
  // rather than a giveaway.
  return html`<div class="quiz-answer">
    <div class="quiz-fb ${ok ? "quiz-ok" : "quiz-no"}">${text}</div>
    <figure class="quiz-plot">
      <figcaption>${ccPick}</figcaption>
      ${ccDemo[ccPick]()}
    </figure>
  </div>`;
}
```

## Turn the knob yourself {.sim-slide #bins-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 1 · binning
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-plot}
```{webr-r}
#| fig-width: 5.7
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
x <- c(6.0, 10.4, 10.5, 9.0, 7.3, 6.6, 6.9,
       8.2, 7.1, 8.1, 7.9, 6.8, 7.4, 9.5, 8.1,
       13.5, 9.9, 6.9, 11.1, 8.2, 8.0, 7.7,
       7.4, 6.5, 9.5, 8.2, 6.9, 7.2, 8.2, 6.7)
bw <- 1   # <-- bin width
brk <- seq(6, 6 + ceiling(8 / bw) * bw, bw)
hist(x, breaks = brk, col = "#CBD9E6",
     border = "white", las = 1,
     main = paste("bin width =", bw),
     xlab = "R&D spend (% of revenue)")
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Run it with `bw <- 1`, then `0.5`, then `2`. The worksheet asks how many of the thirty spend more than 9%. At which width can you still read the answer off the picture?
:::
